claim: IncV-3xFLAG expressed in HEK293 cells infected with C. trachomatis displays a doublet consisting of a 50 and 60 kDa band on western blot.
source: When subjected to anti-FLAG western blot analysis, we noticed that lysates of HEK293 eukaryotic cells infected with wild-type C. trachomatis overexpressing IncV-3xFLAG displayed a doublet consisting of a 50 and 60 kDa band (Figure 1A, middle lane, 293+Ct).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: IncV-3xFLAG ectopically expressed in HEK293 cells has an apparent molecular weight shifted toward the 60 kDa band.
source: By contrast, IncV-3xFLAG ectopically expressed in HEK293 cells had an apparent molecular weight that was shifted toward the 60 kDa band of the doublet (Figure 1A, left lane, 293)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IncV-3xFLAG expressed in E. coli has an apparent molecular weight equivalent to the 50 kDa band.
source: while IncV-3xFLAG expressed in E. coli had an apparent molecular weight equivalent to the 50 kDa band of the doublet (Figure 1A, right lane, Ec).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IncV is post-translationally modified by a host factor.
source: This result led us to hypothesize that IncV is post-translationally modified by a host factor.
evidence: The hypothesis is based on inference from the observed differences in molecular weight of IncV expressed in different systems.

claim: Lambda phosphatase treatment of IncV-3xFLAG decreases its apparent molecular weight from approximately 60 kDa to approximately 50 kDa.
source: In the absence of λ phosphatase, the apparent molecular weight of IncV-3xFLAG was approximately 60 kDa (Figure 1B, left lane). Upon phosphatase treatment, we observed a decrease in the apparent molecular weight of IncV-3xFLAG to approximately 50 kDa, similar to what was observed when IncV-3xFLAG was expressed in E. coli (Figure 1B, right lane).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IncV is phosphorylated by a host cell kinase.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that overexpressed IncV is phosphorylated by a host cell kinase.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from phosphatase assays and molecular weight shifts.

claim: All three subunits of Protein Kinase CK2 were identified as potential interacting partners of IncV in an Inc-human interactome.
source: All three subunits of Protein Kinase CK2 were identified as potential interacting partners of IncV in an Inc-human interactome (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: YFP-CK2α and YFP-CK2β are undetectable at the inclusion in the absence of IncV-3xFLAG expression.
source: In the absence of IncV-3xFLAG expression, YFP-CK2α and YFP-CK2β were undetectable at the inclusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, −aTc).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon overexpression of IncV-3xFLAG, YFP-CK2α and YFP-CK2β are recruited to the inclusion membrane and colocalize with IncV.
source: However, upon overexpression of IncV-3xFLAG, YFP-CK2α, and YFP-CK2β was recruited to the inclusion membrane and colocalized with IncV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, +aTc).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous CK2β colocalizes with IncV at the inclusion when IncV-3xFLAG expression is induced.
source: To confirm that this phenotype was not the result of overexpression of the CK2 subunits, we used antibodies that recognized the endogenous CK2β subunit and showed that endogenous CK2β colocalized with IncV at the inclusion, when IncV-3xFLAG expression was induced (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CK2 is a novel component of ER-Inclusion MCS that is recruited to the inclusion in an IncV-dependent manner.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that CK2 is a novel component of ER-Inclusion MCS that is recruited to the inclusion in an IncV-dependent manner.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data showing CK2 localization to the inclusion in the presence of IncV.

claim: CK2 directly phosphorylates IncV in vitro.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that CK2 directly phosphorylates IncV in vitro.
evidence: The conclusion is based on in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GST-IncV167–363 is phosphorylated in the presence of both ATPγS and CK2.
source: However, in the presence of both ATPγS and CK2, GST-IncV167–363 was phosphorylated (Figure 1D, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IncV phosphorylation is required for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
source: However, this interaction was only detected when IncV167–363 was produced in eukaryotic cells, which, based on the above results, led us to hypothesize that IncV phosphorylation is required for the IncV–VAP interaction.
evidence: The hypothesis is based on inference from previous observations and experimental data.

claim: Untreated IncV-3xFLAG is pulled down by GST-VAPMSP but not by GST alone.
source: Untreated IncV-3xFLAG was pulled down by GST-VAPMSP but not by GST alone, demonstrating a specific interaction between IncV and VAP (Figure 2B, lanes 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lambda phosphatase treatment of IncV-3xFLAG prior to incubation with GST-VAPMSP prevents their interaction.
source: However, when the eluate containing IncV-3xFLAG was treated with λ phosphatase prior to incubation with GST-VAPMSP, the two proteins failed to interact (Figure 2B, lane 4), indicating that phosphorylation of IncV is necessary for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phosphorylation of IncV is necessary for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
source: indicating that phosphorylation of IncV is necessary for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from phosphatase treatment and binding assays.

claim: Phosphorylation of IncV by CK2 is sufficient to promote the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
source: However, when GST-IncV167–363 was treated with CK2 and ATP prior to GST-pull-down, MBP-VAPMSP and GST-IncV167-363 co-immuno-precipitated, indicating that phosphorylation of IncV by CK2 is sufficient to promote the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro (Figure 2D, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IncV phosphorylation is necessary and sufficient for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that IncV phosphorylation is necessary and sufficient for the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from multiple in vitro binding assays.

claim: CK2 is essential for cell viability.
source: Because CK2 is essential (Buchou et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004), we favored a gene silencing approach over a CRISPR-based knockout approach.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of CK2β leads to the appearance of additional bands of intermediate apparent molecular weight for IncV.
source: In contrast, depletion of CK2β led to the appearance of additional bands of intermediate apparent molecular weight (Figure 3A, top and middle blots, pool, A, B, C, D lanes, oo).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CK2β depletion results in the formation of hypophosphorylated species of IncV.
source: A similar analysis of the banding pattern of IncV upon CK2β depletion, with the pooled or individual siRNA duplexes, revealed the appearance of intermediate peaks between the top and bottom bands, suggesting the formation of hypophosphorylated species of IncV (Figure 3B, middle peaks, oo).
evidence: The claim is supported by line scan analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CK2 mediates IncV phosphorylation during infection.
source: These results provided a first indication that CK2 mediates IncV phosphorylation during infection.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from CK2β depletion experiments.

claim: CK2 inhibitor CX-4945 leads to dose-dependent decrease in the apparent molecular weight of IncV.
source: The apparent molecular weight of IncV decreased in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C, top blot), leading to an apparent molecular weight corresponding to unphosphorylated IncV at the 10 μM concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CK2 activity is essential for IncV phosphorylation during infection.
source: These results demonstrate that CK2 activity is essential for IncV phosphorylation during infection.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from CK2 inhibition experiments.

claim: CX-4945 does not interfere with IncV translocation and insertion into the inclusion membrane.
source: Qualitative and quantitative assessment of the micrographs indicated that CX-4945 did not interfere with IncV translocation and insertion into the inclusion membrane (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pretreatment with 10 µM of CX-4945 abolishes VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
source: In comparison, pretreatment of the cells with 10 µM of CX-4945 abolished VAP recruitment to the inclusion (Figure 3D, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Phosphorylation of IncV by CK2 is required for the IncV-dependent VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that phosphorylation of IncV by CK2 is required for the IncV-dependent VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from CK2 inhibition and microscopy experiments.

claim: CX-4945 does not interfere with CK2 association with the inclusion.
source: Qualitative and quantitative assessment of the micrographs indicated that CX-4945 did not interfere with CK2 association with the inclusion (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: CK2 kinase activity is dispensable for the IncV-dependent CK2 localization to the inclusion.
source: Thus, CK2 kinase activity is dispensable for the IncV-dependent CK2 localization to the inclusion.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data showing CK2 localization in the presence of CK2 inhibitor.

claim: CX-4945 washout after CK2 association with the inclusion leads to robust VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
source: In comparison, CX-4945 washout post CK2 association with the inclusion, led to a robust VAP recruitment to the inclusion, similar to the one observed in the absence of CX-4945 (Figure 4D, E, compare CX-4945 washout to No CX-4945).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4D, E.

claim: The IncV-dependent CK2 association with the inclusion does not require CK2 kinase activity and precedes VAP recruitment, which requires an active CK2 kinase.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the IncV-dependent CK2 association with the inclusion does not require CK2 kinase activity and precedes VAP recruitment, which requires an active CK2 kinase.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from CK2 inhibition and washout experiments.

claim: A C-terminal region of IncV between amino acids 342 and 356 is required for the IncV-dependent CK2 recruitment to the inclusion.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that a C-terminal region of IncV, between amino acids 342 and 356, is required for the IncV-dependent CK2 recruitment to the inclusion and subsequent VAP association with the inclusion.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from truncation mutant analysis.

claim: The cytosolic domain of IncV contains seven CK2 recognition motifs.
source: The primary amino acid structure of the IncV domain necessary for CK2 recruitment (342SSESSDEESSSDSS356) contains seven CK2 recognition motifs (S/T-x-x-D/E/pS/pY) (Litchfield, 2003; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and citation to a previous study defining CK2 recognition motifs.

claim: Three CK2 recognition motifs in IncV do not require priming by phosphorylation.
source: Three of them do not require priming by phosphorylation of the fourth serine or tyrosine residue and could result in the direct CK2-dependent phosphorylation of IncV on serine residues S345, S346, and S350, hereby facilitating the assembly of the IncV–VAP tether.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of CK2 recognition motif sequences and inference about phosphorylation.

claim: IncVS3A expression results in a significant decrease in both CK2β and VAP recruitment to the inclusion compared to IncVWT.
source: However, qualitative and quantitative analysis revealed that in comparison to IncVWT-3xFLAG, IncVS3A-3xFLAG expression resulted in a significant decrease in both CK2β and VAP recruitment to the inclusion (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: Serine residues S345, S346, and S350 located in a C-terminal motif of IncV are critical for CK2 and VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that serine residues S345, S346, and S350 located in a C-terminal motif of IncV, are critical for CK2 and VAP recruitment to the inclusion.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from alanine substitution mutant analysis.

claim: IncVS3A is unphosphorylated.
source: These results indicated that IncVS3A is unphosphorylated.
evidence: The conclusion is based on western blot data showing IncVS3A has the same apparent molecular weight as unphosphorylated IncV.

claim: IncVS3A expression leads to a significant reduction of ER-Inclusion MCS formation compared to IncVWT.
source: Additionally, quantification of the proportion of inclusion membrane associated with the ER indicated a significant reduction of ER-Inclusion MCS formation upon IncVS3A expression, compared to IncVWT (Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: CK2-dependent phosphorylation of IncV controls assembly of the IncV–VAP tether and ER-Inclusion MCS formation.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the CK2-dependent phosphorylation of IncV controls assembly of the IncV–VAP tether and ER-Inclusion MCS formation.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from mutant analysis and electron microscopy.

claim: Phosphorylation of S345, S346, and S350 alone is not sufficient to promote VAP binding in vitro.
source: While we cannot exclude that the phosphomimetic mutations failed to mimic phosphorylation, these results indicated that, although critical for CK2 recruitment, IncV hyperphosphorylation status, and assembly of the IncV–VAP tether at the ER-inclusion MCS, phosphorylation of S345, S346, and S350 alone is not sufficient to promote VAP binding in vitro, suggesting that additional IncV phosphorylation sites are required to promote optimal interaction between IncV and VAP.
evidence: The conclusion is based on in vitro binding assay data with phosphomimetic mutants.

claim: IncV displays one noncanonical (262S1F2H3T4P5P6N7268) and one canonical FFAT motif (286E1Y2M3D4A5L6E7292).
source: We have previously shown that IncV displays one noncanonical (262S1F2H3T4P5P6N7268) and one canonical FFAT motif (286E1Y2M3D4A5L6E7292) (Figure 6A; Stanhope et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Alanine substitution of residue in position 2 of each FFAT motif, individually and in combination, led to partial and full reduction of the IncV–VAP interaction, respectively.
source: In agreement with position 2 of a FFAT motif being a phenylalanine or a tyrosine residue critical for VAP–FFAT interactions (Kawano et al., 2006; Loewen et al., 2003), we had shown that alanine substitution of residue in position 2 of each motif, individually (IncVF263A or IncVY287A) and in combination (IncVF263A/Y287A), led to a partial and full reduction of the IncV–VAP interaction, respectively, indicating that both FFAT motifs cooperate for VAP binding (Stanhope et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The noncanonical FFAT motif of IncV contains a phosphorylatable threonine residue in position 4 (T265).
source: The presence of a phosphorylatable threonine residue in position 4 of the noncanonical FFAT motif of IncV (T265) (Figure 6A) suggests that, as proposed by Di Mattia et al., the noncanonical FFAT of IncV could be a phospho-FFAT motif.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A and inference from literature.

claim: IncVT265A and IncVT265A/Y287A exhibit partial and complete loss of VAP association with the inclusion, respectively.
source: Similarly, IncVT265A and IncVT265A/Y287A exhibited partial and complete loss of VAP association with the inclusion, respectively (Figure 6B, C) indicating that substitution of T265 to a nonphosphorylatable residue impacted the ability of the noncanonical FFAT motif to mediate the VAP–FFAT interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B, C.

claim: IncVT265D/P266A results in VAP inclusion association similar to IncVWT.
source: On the contrary, IncVT265D/P266A resulted in VAP inclusion association similar to IncVWT, indicating that phosphomimetic mutation of IncV noncanonical FFAT resulted in optimal VAP binding during infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: CK2 and S345, S346, and S350 play an indirect role in the phosphorylation of T265 in the IncV noncanonical FFAT motif.
source: These results indicate that CK2 and S345, S346, and S350 play an indirect role in the phosphorylation of T265 in the IncV noncanonical FFAT motif.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from phosphomimetic mutant analysis.

claim: Phosphorylation of T265 of IncV noncanonical FFAT is indirectly controlled by CK2 and contributes to the IncV–VAP interaction.
source: Altogether, because of inconclusive results with the VAPK50L mutant, it remains unclear if IncV noncanonical FFAT acts as a phospho-FFAT. However, the above results indicate that phosphorylation of T265 of IncV noncanonical FFAT is indirectly controlled by CK2 and contributes, but is not sufficient, to mediate the IncV–VAP interaction, suggesting that additional residues must be phosphorylated to ensure full IncV–VAP interaction.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from multiple mutant analyses.

claim: The primary amino acid structures upstream of the IncV FFAT motifs are highly enriched in phosphorylatable serine residues.
source: We noted that, instead of typical acidic residues, the primary amino acid structures upstream of the IncV FFAT motifs are highly enriched in phosphorylatable serine residues (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expression of IncVS/A-3xFLAG results in a significant decrease in YFP-VAP recruitment to the inclusion compared to IncVWT-3xFLAG.
source: Qualitative and quantitative analysis revealed that expression of IncVS/A-3xFLAG resulted in a significant decrease in YFP-VAP recruitment to the inclusion as observed with IncVF263A/Y287A-3xFLAG and compared to IncVWT-3xFLAG (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7B, C.

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation of the serine-rich tracts is sufficient to promote the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
source: However, we observed a 20-fold increase in VAPMSP binding to IncVS/D compared to IncVWT (Figure 7D, lane 3), indicating that phosphomimetic mutation of the serine-rich tracts is sufficient to promote the IncV–VAP interaction in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Phosphorylated serine-rich tracts located upstream of IncV FFAT motifs are both necessary and sufficient for promoting the IncV–VAP interaction.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that instead of typical acidic tracts, phosphorylated serine-rich tracts located upstream of IncV FFAT motifs are both necessary and sufficient for promoting the IncV–VAP interaction.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data from mutant analysis and in vitro binding assays.

claim: IncVS/D-3xFLAG remains trapped within the bacteria and does not localize to the inclusion membrane.
source: In comparison to IncVWT and all other mutated alleles used in this study, IncVS/D-3xFLAG remained trapped within the bacteria and did not localize to the inclusion membrane (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Phosphorylatable serine residues may have been selected over acidic residues to allow proper Type III translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane.
source: These results suggest that phosphorylatable serine residues may have been selected over acidic residues to allow proper Type III translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane.
evidence: The conclusion is based on inference from experimental data showing IncVS/D fails to translocate.

claim: Unphosphorylated IncV is translocated across the inclusion membrane by the T3SS.
source: Unphosphorylated IncV is translocated across the inclusion membrane by the T3SS.
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: Upon insertion into the inclusion membrane and exposure to the cytosol, IncV recruits the host kinase CK2 through a C-terminal domain containing three serine residues (S345, S346, and S350).
source: Upon insertion into the inclusion membrane and exposure to the cytosol (Figure 8, Step 1), IncV recruits the host kinase CK2 through a C-terminal domain containing three serine residues (S345, S346, and S350) that are part of CK2 recognition sites (Figure 8, Step 2).
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: IncV becomes hyperphosphorylated, including phosphorylation of T265 of the noncanonical FFAT and serine tracts directly upstream of the FFAT motifs.
source: As a consequence, IncV becomes hyperphosphorylated, including phosphorylation of T265 of the noncanonical FFAT and serine tracts directly upstream of the FFAT motifs (Figure 8, Step 3).
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: IncV phosphorylation leads to IncV interaction with VAP, tether assembly, and ER-Inclusion MCS formation.
source: These phosphorylation events lead to IncV interaction with VAP, tether assembly, and ER-Inclusion MCS formation (Figure 8, Step 4).
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: Additional kinases must contribute to IncV hyperphosphorylation, especially for phosphorylation of T265.
source: Our data are consistent with CK2 playing a central role in initiating IncV hyperphosphorylation (Figure 8, Step 2), however, additional kinases must contribute, especially for phosphorylation of T265 (Figure 8, Step 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing T265 is not a CK2 target.

claim: Post-translocation phosphorylation of IncV ensures optimal VAP binding while preserving proper T3SS-mediated translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane.
source: Importantly, the post-translocation phosphorylation of IncV ensures optimal VAP binding while preserving proper T3SS-mediated translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane.
evidence: The conclusion is based on experimental data showing IncVS/D fails to translocate.

claim: Membrane contact sites (MCS) are crucial for nonvesicular trafficking-based interorganelle communication.
source: Membrane contact sites (MCS) are crucial for nonvesicular trafficking-based interorganelle communication.
evidence: This is a general statement about MCS based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: ER–organelle tethering occurs in part through the interaction of the ER resident protein VAP with FFAT motif-containing proteins.
source: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–organelle tethering occurs in part through the interaction of the ER resident protein VAP with FFAT motif-containing proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement about ER-organelle tethering based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: FFAT motifs are characterized by a seven amino acidic core surrounded by acid tracks.
source: FFAT motifs are characterized by a seven amino acidic core surrounded by acid tracks.
evidence: This is a general statement about FFAT motifs based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: C. trachomatis establishes MCS between its vacuole (the inclusion) and the ER through expression of a bacterial tether, IncV, displaying molecular mimicry of eukaryotic FFAT motif cores.
source: We have previously shown that the human intracellular bacterial pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis establishes MCS between its vacuole (the inclusion) and the ER through expression of a bacterial tether, IncV, displaying molecular mimicry of eukaryotic FFAT motif cores.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Multiple layers of host cell kinase-mediated phosphorylation events govern the assembly of the IncV–VAP tethering complex and the formation of ER-Inclusion MCS.
source: Here, we show that multiple layers of host cell kinase-mediated phosphorylation events govern the assembly of the IncV–VAP tethering complex and the formation of ER-Inclusion MCS.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings of the study.

claim: IncV recruits CK2 to the inclusion leading to IncV hyperphosphorylation of the noncanonical FFAT motif core and serine-rich tracts immediately upstream of IncV FFAT motif cores.
source: Via a C-terminal region containing three CK2 phosphorylation motifs, IncV recruits CK2 to the inclusion leading to IncV hyperphosphorylation of the noncanonical FFAT motif core and serine-rich tracts immediately upstream of IncV FFAT motif cores.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings of the study.

claim: Phosphorylatable serine tracts, rather than genetically encoded acidic tracts, accommodate Type III-mediated translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane, while achieving full mimicry of FFAT motifs.
source: Phosphorylatable serine tracts, rather than genetically encoded acidic tracts, accommodate Type III-mediated translocation of IncV to the inclusion membrane, while achieving full mimicry of FFAT motifs.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings of the study.

claim: Regulatory components and post-translational modifications are integral to MCS biology.
source: Thus, regulatory components and post-translational modifications are integral to MCS biology, and intracellular pathogens such as C. trachomatis have evolved complex molecular mimicry of these eukaryotic features.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: Intracellular pathogens such as C. trachomatis have evolved complex molecular mimicry of eukaryotic MCS regulatory features.
source: Thus, regulatory components and post-translational modifications are integral to MCS biology, and intracellular pathogens such as C. trachomatis have evolved complex molecular mimicry of these eukaryotic features.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: MCS are points of contact between the membrane of two adjacent organelles (10–30 nm apart).
source: In naive cells, membrane contact sites (MCS) are points of contact between the membrane of two adjacent organelles (10–30 nm apart).
evidence: This is a general statement about MCS based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: MCS provide physical platforms for the nonvesicular transfer of lipids and ions, and cell signaling events important for interorganelle communication and organelle positioning and dynamics.
source: They provide physical platforms for the nonvesicular transfer of lipids and ions, and cell signaling events important for interorganelle communication and organelle positioning and dynamics (Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about MCS function based on citation to a review.

claim: MCS dysfunction has been linked to several human diseases.
source: Since their discovery and implication in cell homeostasis, MCS dysfunction has been linked to several human diseases (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Castro et al., 2018; Stoica et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each MCS is enriched in specific proteinaceous factors that contribute to the specialized biological function of a given MCS.
source: At the molecular level, depending on the contacting organelles [endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–Golgi, ER–mitochondria, ER–plasma membrane (PM), etc.], each MCS is enriched in specific proteinaceous factors that contribute to the specialized biological function of a given MCS (Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review.

claim: MCS components form tethering complexes that increase the affinity of one organelle to another and keep their membranes in close proximity.
source: By bridging the membrane of apposed organelles, either via protein–protein or protein–lipid interactions, MCS components also form tethering complexes that increase the affinity of one organelle to another and thereby keep their membranes in close proximity (Eisenberg-Bord et al., 2016; Prinz et al., 2020; Scorrano et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VAP engages in tethering complexes at several MCS by interaction with proteins containing FFAT motifs.
source: Although the overall molecular composition of each MCS is different, one integral ER protein, the vesicle-associated membrane protein (VAMP)-associated protein (VAP) (Murphy and Levine, 2016), engages in tethering complexes at several MCS. This is accomplished by interaction of the cytosolic major sperm protein (MSP) domain of VAP with proteins containing two phenylalanine in an acidic tract (FFAT) motifs (Loewen et al., 2003; Murphy and Levine, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FFAT motif-containing proteins include soluble proteins and transmembrane proteins anchored to the contacting organelle.
source: FFAT motif-containing proteins include soluble proteins, such as lipid transfer proteins that contain an additional domain for targeting to the opposing membrane, and transmembrane proteins anchored to the contacting organelle (James and Kehlenbach, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review.

claim: A consensus of the FFAT motif core was first defined as seven amino acids, E1F2F3D4A5x6E7.
source: A consensus of the FFAT motif core was first defined as seven amino acids, E1F2F3D4A5x6E7; however, the core motif of many identified VAP interacting proteins deviates from this canonical sequence (James and Kehlenbach, 2021; Loewen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acidic residues surrounding the core motif are proposed to facilitate the VAP–FFAT interaction through electrostatic interactions.
source: In addition to the core, acidic residues surrounding the core motif are proposed to facilitate the VAP–FFAT interaction through electrostatic interactions (Furuita et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MCS are exploited by intracellular pathogens for replication.
source: In addition to their critical role in interorganelle communication, MCS are exploited by intracellular pathogens for replication (Derré, 2017; Ishikawa-Sasaki et al., 2018; Justis et al., 2017; McCune et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: C. trachomatis is the causative agent of the most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection.
source: One example is the obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, the causative agent of the most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection.
evidence: This is a general statement about C. trachomatis based on established knowledge.

claim: C. trachomatis replicates within a membrane-bound vacuole called the inclusion.
source: Upon invasion of the genital epithelium, C. trachomatis replicates within a membrane-bound vacuole called the inclusion (Gitsels et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Maturation of the inclusion relies on Chlamydia effector proteins that are translocated across the inclusion membrane via a bacterially encoded Type III secretion system.
source: Maturation of the inclusion relies on Chlamydia effector proteins that are translocated across the inclusion membrane via a bacterially encoded Type III secretion system (Lara-Tejero and Galán, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inclusion membrane proteins (Inc) are inserted into the inclusion membrane and are strategically positioned to mediate inclusion interactions with host cell organelles.
source: A subset of Chlamydia Type III effector proteins, known as the inclusion membrane proteins (Inc), are inserted into the inclusion membrane and are therefore strategically positioned to mediate inclusion interactions with host cell organelles (Bugalhão and Mota, 2019; Dehoux et al., 2011; Lutter et al., 2012; Moore and Ouellette, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Points of contact between the ER and the inclusion membrane are referred to as ER-Inclusion MCS based on their similarities to MCS between cellular organelles.
source: These interactions include points of contact between the ER and the inclusion membrane, without membrane fusion (Derré et al., 2011; Dumoux et al., 2012), which are referred to as ER-Inclusion MCS based on their similarities to MCS between cellular organelles (Agaisse and Derré, 2015; Derré et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IncV constitutes a structural component that tethers the ER membrane to the inclusion membrane through interaction with VAP.
source: Characterization of the protein composition of ER-Inclusion MCS led to the identification the Inc protein IncV, which constitutes a structural component that tethers the ER membrane to the inclusion membrane through interaction with VAP (Stanhope et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The IncV–VAP interaction relies on the presence of two FFAT motifs in the C-terminal cytosolic tail of IncV.
source: The IncV–VAP interaction relies on the presence of two FFAT motifs in the C-terminal cytosolic tail of IncV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The residue in position 2 in each FFAT motif of IncV (Y287 and F263) is essential for the IncV–VAP interaction during infection.
source: Similar to eukaryotic FFAT, the residue in position 2 in each motif (Y287 and F263, respectively) is essential for the IncV–VAP interaction during infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Chlamydia evolved a post-translocation phosphorylation strategy to accommodate proper secretion via the Type III secretion system while achieving full mimicry of eukaryotic FFAT motifs.
source: Since the substitution for genetically encoded acidic tracts interfered with IncV translocation, we propose that Chlamydia evolved a post-translocation phosphorylation strategy in order to accommodate proper secretion via the Type III secretion system, while achieving full mimicry of eukaryotic FFAT motifs.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: Few kinases phosphorylating VAP-dependent tethers have been identified.
source: Few kinases phosphorylating VAP-dependent tethers have been identified (Kors et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020) and how they associate with MCS to phosphorylate their target has not been explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alanine substitution of S345, S346, and S350 eliminates an essential docking site for subsequent CK2-mediated phosphorylation of distal residues in the cytosolic domain of IncV.
source: We therefore propose that alanine substitution of S345, S346, and S350 eliminates an essential docking site for subsequent CK2-mediated phosphorylation of distal residues in the cytosolic domain of IncV, including the serine tracts next to the FFAT motifs (see below).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The study may have identified CK2 as a regulator of cellular MCS.
source: Moreover, since intracellular pathogens often mimic cellular processes, our study may have identified CK2 as a regulator of cellular MCS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: Di Mattia et al. identified a new class of FFAT motifs referred to as phospho-FFAT motifs in which the acidic residue in position 4 is replaced by a phosphorylatable residue.
source: Recently, Di Mattia et al. identified a new class of FFAT motifs referred to as phospho-FFAT motifs in which the acidic residue in position 4 is replaced by a phosphorylatable residue, such as serine or threonine (Di Mattia et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence of a phospho-FFAT in IncV would add to the growing list of proteins that interact with VAP via a phospho-FFAT.
source: The presence of a phospho-FFAT in IncV would add to the growing list of proteins that interact with VAP via a phospho-FFAT. These include STARD3 at ER–endosome contacts, the potassium channel Kv.2 at ER–PM contacts in neurons, Miga at ERMCS, and VPS13D at ER–mitochondria MCS (Di Mattia et al., 2020; Guillén-Samander et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A putative phospho-FFAT in the norovirus protein NS2 is essential for interaction with VAP and viral replication.
source: Moreover, although not recognized as such at the time, a putative phospho-FFAT in the norovirus protein NS2 is essential for interaction with VAP and viral replication (McCune et al., 2017), indicating that this mechanism of interaction with VAP might also be conserved amongst pathogens.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study and inference.

claim: In the context of STARD3-dependent formation of ER–endosome contacts, the presence of a single phospho-FFAT is proposed to act as a molecular switch to regulate contact formation.
source: In the context of the STARD3-dependent formation of ER–endosome contacts, the presence of a single phospho-FFAT is proposed to act as a molecular switch to regulate contact formation (Di Mattia et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphorylation of a single serine residue six amino acids upstream of the CERT FFAT motif (S315) enhances the CERT–VAP interaction.
source: The phosphorylation, by an unknown kinase, of a single serine residue six amino acids upstream of the CERT FFAT motif (S315) enhances the CERT–VAP interaction (Kumagai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphorylation of three serine residues directly upstream of the FFAT-like motif of ACBD5 promotes VAP binding and peroxisome–ER contacts formation.
source: Similarly, the phosphorylation of three serine residues directly upstream of the FFAT-like motif of ACBD5 promotes VAP binding and peroxisome–ER contacts formation (Kors et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Six serine residues spread over 21 residues upstream of the core FFAT motif of Miga facilitate the Miga–VAP interaction.
source: Another example are six serine residues, spread over 21 residues upstream of the core FFAT motif of Miga, shown to facilitate the Miga–VAP interaction (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: At least two kinases CKI and CaMKII were required for Miga phosphorylation.
source: At least two kinases CKI and CaMKII were required for Miga phosphorylation; however, other kinases are likely involved (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: IncV is the first example of a FFAT motif-containing protein that displays serine tracts in place of acidic tracts.
source: IncV is the first example of a FFAT motif-containing protein that displays serine tracts in place of acidic tracts.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the findings of the study and comparison to known FFAT motif-containing proteins.

claim: If built into the available FFAT motif identification algorithms, the feature of serine tracts could potentially reveal additional cellular VAP interacting proteins.
source: If built into the available FFAT motif identification algorithms, this feature could potentially reveal additional cellular VAP interacting proteins (Di Mattia et al., 2020; Murphy and Levine, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the findings.

claim: Tracks of aspartic acid or glutamic acid residues may interfere with Type III secretion.
source: In the case of Chlamydia Inc proteins, it is possible that tracks of aspartic acid or glutamic acid residues would create an excess of negative charges that may interfere with Type III secretion.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Chlamydia IncV is no longer properly translocated to the inclusion membrane when the serine tracts are mutated to aspartic acid residues.
source: In support of this notion, we found that Chlamydia IncV is no longer properly translocated to the inclusion membrane when the serine tracts are mutated to aspartic acid residues, and instead remains trapped within the bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The recruitment of a phosphatase to ER-Inclusion MCS may contribute to the disassembly of IncV–VAP tethers.
source: In addition, we cannot exclude the possibility that the recruitment of a phosphatase to ER-Inclusion MCS may contribute to the disassembly of IncV–VAP tethers, as shown for the calcineurin-dependent disassembly of Kv.2-VAP ER–PM contacts in neurons (Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to another system.

claim: A combination of host cell kinases and phosphatases could regulate the dynamics of ER-Inclusion contact sites during the Chlamydia developmental cycle.
source: A combination of host cell kinases and phosphatases could thus regulate the dynamics of ER-Inclusion contact sites during the Chlamydia developmental cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential regulatory mechanisms.
